content: Blurred vision is a frequent ocular symptom characterized by a sudden or gradual reduction in the clarity or sharpness of vision, making it difficult to perceive fine details. It can affect one eye (unilateral) or both eyes (bilateral). There is limited historical information available regarding blurred vision. Currently, there is no standardized system for classifying blurred vision. The underlying mechanisms of blurred vision may involve refractive errors, opacities in ocular structures such as the lens, cornea, or vitreous, retinal disorders, or diseases affecting the optic nerve. Blurred vision can arise from a variety of ocular and systemic conditions, including but not limited to: Refractive errors (the most common cause) Age-related macular degeneration Cataracts Presbyopia Diabetic retinopathy Glaucoma Corneal abrasions, scarring, or keratitis Conjunctivitis Uveitis or iritis Retinal detachment Retinitis Ocular trauma, such as hyphema Migraines Malignancies or tumors (e.g., brain tumors, metastatic lung cancer, leukemia) Optic neuritis Cerebrovascular diseases, including transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) and strokes Vasculitis, such as temporal arteritis or systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) Hypertension Side effects of medications Blurred vision can occur in individuals of all age groups. Risk factors for developing blurred vision include genetic predisposition, family history of ocular conditions, diabetes mellitus, advanced age, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension. Screening recommendations include: Comprehensive eye examinations for patients with type 1 diabetes within five years of diagnosis and at the time of diagnosis for those with type 2 diabetes, with annual follow-ups thereafter. Insufficient evidence exists to recommend routine glaucoma screening, but individuals at higher risk (e.g., African Americans, older adults) should consult their healthcare provider. The prognosis of blurred vision depends on the underlying cause. Complications and outcomes vary widely based on the specific etiology. There are no universally established diagnostic criteria for blurred vision. Diagnosis relies on a thorough medical history and a detailed eye examination. Key aspects of the history include the onset, duration, associated symptoms, and whether the condition is unilateral or bilateral. Common symptoms accompanying blurred vision include eye redness, pain, excessive tearing (epiphora), headaches, light sensitivity (photophobia), halos around lights, nausea, excessive thirst (polydipsia), frequent urination (polyuria), dizziness, and numbness. Physical examination involves: Visual acuity testing Visual field assessment Slit-lamp examination Ophthalmoscopy Tonometry Gonioscopy (angle testing) Neurological symptoms such as sudden hemiplegia, abnormal gait, ataxia, or dysarthria may indicate a cerebrovascular accident. Laboratory investigations may include: Blood glucose and HbA1c levels for diabetes-related blurred vision Urinalysis and renal function tests for hypertensive patients Antinuclear antibodies and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) for SLE or vasculitis Complete blood count (CBC) and other tests for conditions like leukemia or multiple myeloma Imaging studies may include: CT scans to identify mass lesions or ischemic/hemorrhagic strokes MRI to confirm optic nerve inflammation or other structural abnormalities Treatment depends on the underlying cause: Refractive errors and presbyopia are managed with corrective lenses or eyeglasses. Supportive care for hyphema includes elevating the head of the bed, using an eye shield, and reducing physical activity. Dry macular degeneration has no definitive treatment, while wet macular degeneration may be managed with anti-VEGF medications or photodynamic therapy. Diabetic retinopathy is treated with anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenesis agents (e.g., anti-VEGF drugs), laser therapy, or vitrectomy. Glaucoma is managed with pharmacologic therapy (e.g., eye drops) or surgical interventions such as trabeculoplasty, iridotomy, or trabeculectomy. Infectious causes are treated with antibacterial, antiviral, or antiparasitic agents. Corticosteroids are used for uveitis, iritis, optic neuritis, and temporal arteritis. Hypertension is treated with antihypertensive medications. Surgical options include: LASIK for refractive errors Cataract surgery Retinal detachment repair Vitrectomy for diabetic retinopathy Primary prevention strategies for diabetic retinopathy include maintaining a healthy lifestyle, controlling hypertension, managing lipid levels, and undergoing regular ophthalmic examinations. These interventions may involve weight management, antihypertensive therapy, statins, antiplatelet agents, diabetes management, and smoking cessation.
